full_judgment:
2. The petitioner made an application for pre-empting the land of which she a cushier and it was sold by her co-sharer Nasamon Bibi to opposite party No. 1 at Rs. 1,000/- by a registered kabala dated 14.3.62. She stated that she received no notice of sale. She came to know about the sale in August, 1963 and then she took a copy of the kabala and filed the application (on 23.9.63) for pre-emption with deposit of necessary money. The Courts below have found that she has not been able to prove that her knowledge was within the period of limitation as given in section 96 of the East Bengal Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act i.e. four months. 

 3. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule, has firstly contended that the period of limitation in this particular case should be as given in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act in view of the fact that operation of section 96 of the Act which occurs in Part V of the Act become effective on 1st August, 1963. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied upon a notification No. SA-116/63/609/8th July, 1963 published in the 'Dacca Gazette', Part 1 page 1169. The notification reads as follows:— 

 "In exercise of the powers conferred by section 79 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act XXVIII of 1951), the Governor is pleased to direct that Part V of the said Act shall come into force in the following districts with effect from the date of publication of this notification (i.e., from the 1st August, 1963): 

 4. This notification clearly shows that operation of Part V of the Act in the district of Rajshahi where this case originated becomes effective from 1st August, 1963. The application was made from the date of her knowledge in August, 1963 and the application was filed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on 23.9.63. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin then submits that his right to pre-empt accrued under the Bengal Tenancy Act and that rule of three years limitation should be followed in this particular case. In this connection, the learned Advocate has relied upon the decision in the case of Abdul Malek Vs. Abdur Rahman reported in 19 Dacca Law Reports (Dacca) page 318. It has been held in that case that section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act applying rule of three years limitation from the date of knowledge will govern the present case in view of section 8 of the General Clauses Act. The same view has also been expressed in another case reported in the same volume at page 615. In this case, it has been held :— 

 "It is a settled rule of interpretation that when one statute repeals another, the repealing statute is to be so construed as not to affect retrospectively the right accrued or acquired under the repealed statute unless such construction appears clearly in the terms of the repealing statute or arises by necessary implication. There is nothing in section 96 of the State Acquisition Act to indicate that it took away or impaired the right of pre-emption accrued under that the repealed section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, either expressly or by necessary implication." 

 5. In view of the decisions cited above, it is quite clear that the application for pre-emption has been made within the time allowed under section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The Courts below did not get the benefit of the decisions cited from 19 Dacca Law Reports, inasmuch as, the decision of the lower appellate Court was on 27.2.67 and the 19 Dacca Law Reports was published later in 1967. In the circumstances, the application is allowed and the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order of the Courts below are set aside.
